title: The Pale Portrait
premise: Folklorist Noor Coldharbour arrives in the drowned village of Marrowfen to record songs the locals refuse to sing twice, and discovers every photograph from her late grandmother's house has gained an extra chair — pulled to the center of the frame, waiting. The chair is an invitation, and Noor realizes her grandmother once answered it, binding the family to the Hollow Guest that the village has fed with silence for a century. As the nights shorten and neighbors who 'count the doors' begin to die in the order of the songs, Noor must choose between the loyalty that kept Marrowfen's pact alive and the truth that could break it. In the end she sings the forbidden verse aloud at sunrise, naming the Guest and dissolving the pact — freeing the village but erasing her grandmother from every photograph, memory, and song, leaving Noor the only one who remembers her at all.
about_author: Marguerite Ravensworth is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing orphaned photographs in county records offices, a job that left her convinced images keep their own ledgers. She writes horror about inheritance, obligation, and the things families agree never to say aloud.

chapters.title: Songs Not Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Arriving in fogbound Marrowfen, she records a washerwoman's lullaby and watches the woman's face drain when Noor asks her to repeat it. The village's warmth curdles into watchful courtesy. Beat: unease planted beneath welcome.

chapters.title: The House That Counts Its Doors
chapters.summary: Noor inherits her grandmother Edith's cottage and finds chalk tallies beside every door, refreshed daily by someone unknown. A neighbor, Bram Tull, warns her to keep the tallies current. Beat: dread of inherited duty.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Sorting Edith's photographs, she finds a plain wooden chair standing at the center of every image, including shots taken decades apart. In the newest photo — taken last week — the chair faces the camera. Beat: uncanny intrusion.

chapters.title: Nobody Sings the Fourth Verse
chapters.summary: At the village pub, a fiddler plays a harvest song and stops cold at verse four. Old men leave. Bram explains only that the fourth verse 'names the listener.' Beat: the shape of a taboo.

chapters.title: Edith's Ledger
chapters.summary: In the attic Noor finds her grandmother's folkloric notebooks — Edith was a folklorist too — with the fourth verse copied out and struck through eleven times. The final entry: 'It knows a Coldharbour is listening.' Beat: inheritance becomes threat.

chapters.title: The Chair Moves Closer
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Overnight the chair in the photographs grows larger; in one, a hand rests on its arm. She burns three photographs; by morning the chair appears in photos of her own flat in the city. Beat: the haunting crosses thresholds.

chapters.title: Doors and Tallies
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram recounts the pact: a century ago Marrowfen invited something in to end a famine, and the tallies and unsung verses keep the invitation 'polite.' He checks Noor's chalk and finds a thirteenth mark no one made. Beat: exposition as confession.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Remembers Singing
chapters.summary: Noor interviews Agnes Pike, the village's oldest resident, who hums the fourth verse in her sleep. Awake, Agnes insists she's never heard it — but describes the tune perfectly. Beat: memory as contested territory.

chapters.title: What the Photographs Want
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The chair now sits before a hearth in every photo, and the hearth fire is lit in images from midsummer. Noor realizes the pictures are converging on a single night: the one ahead, the old pact's anniversary. Beat: a deadline emerges.

chapters.title: A Neighbor Stops Counting
chapters.summary: The washerwoman from chapter one is found dead, her doors chalkless, her face turned toward an empty corner. The village closes ranks; the vicar calls it a weak heart. Beat: first death, first lie.

chapters.title: The Order of the Songs
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Mapping the songs Edith collected against the deaths of their singers, Noor finds they're dying in the order the verses were recorded. The next name on the list is Agnes Pike. Beat: pattern recognized, stakes personal.

chapters.title: Bram's Bargain
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram admits he's been maintaining Edith's tallies since her death, buying time, and offers Noor a choice: leave before the anniversary and the pact passes to another family, or stay and 'sit where invited.' Beat: loyalty framed as a trap.

chapters.title: The Chair in the Mirror
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The chair appears in mirrors now, always empty, always angled so its occupant would face her. She photographs it; the developed image shows a silhouette she doesn't remember being there. Beat: the Guest acquires a body.

chapters.title: Agnes's Confession
chapters.summary: Agnes, lucid and terrified, tells Noor she was a child when Edith recorded the fourth verse — and that Edith sang it back to the village as proof she could be trusted. The Guest has been waiting a lifetime for a Coldharbour to sing it again. Beat: grandmother's complicity revealed.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. In Edith's earliest notebook, Noor reads the famine history: the village starved until Edith's grandmother sang the Guest over the threshold. It fed the fields and fed on the singers, one per generation, chosen by the songs. Beat: the pact's true cost.

chapters.title: The Vicar's Version
chapters.summary: The vicar, smooth and rehearsed, offers Noor the official history — a blessing, a harvest rite, nothing to fear — while quietly removing Edith's name from the church memorial roll. Beat: institutional truth versus lived truth.

chapters.title: Doors Out of Order
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Someone has smeared Noor's tallies. That night every door in the cottage stands open, and the photographs show the chair now placed at her own kitchen table. Beat: the boundary of the house is failing.

chapters.title: Agnes Dies Singing
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Agnes is found at dawn on her doorstep, mid-hum, cold, her own door tallied in a hand that isn't hers. The village holds a funeral where no one weeps and everyone watches Noor. Beat: grief and accusation entwined.

chapters.title: The Inheritance of Blame
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Villagers begin leaving chalk marks on Noor's doors — marking her, not protecting her. She understands: they've decided the Guest may take her in Agnes's place, and their loyalty is to the pact, not to her. Beat: isolation deepens.

chapters.title: The Photograph of Edith
chapters.summary: Noor finds a photo of Edith on the anniversary night forty years ago: Edith seated in the chair, smiling, a second shadow behind her. Written on the back: 'Paid in full. Next: a Coldharbour who listens.' Beat: the debt comes due.

chapters.title: Running Counts as Leaving
chapters.summary: Noor flees to the city, but every photograph she owns now contains the chair, and strangers on the street hum the harvest tune. Bram calls: 'It doesn't chase. It waits where you're going.' Beat: escape revealed as illusion.

chapters.title: The Archive at Midnight
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. In a county archive, Noor finds Marrowfen records: eleven singers taken across a century, each a folklorist or a singer, each 'invited.' The twelfth entry is blank except for her own name in Edith's handwriting. Beat: the trap was generational.

chapters.title: Bram Breaks Ranks
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram, who lost his sister to the pact in the 1980s, confesses he's kept the tallies out of guilt, not loyalty. He gives Noor Edith's missing final notebook and the village's one weapon: the Guest can be named, and naming unbinds — at the namer's cost. Beat: alliance formed; price stated.

chapters.title: What Naming Costs
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Edith's final notebook explains: the one who sings the fourth verse aloud dissolves the pact, but the Guest 'unwrites' what the singer most truly holds. Edith chose silence to keep her granddaughter in the world. Beat: Noor understands her grandmother's love and cowardice at once.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Begins
chapters.summary: Noor returns to Marrowfen at dusk. Doors stand open all down the lane; the villagers, tallies abandoned, wait in their gardens like an audience. The hearth in every photograph is lit. Beat: calm before the long night.

chapters.title: The First Hour
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Barricaded in the cottage, Noor watches the photographs: the chair is now occupied by a figure that is more absence than shape. It doesn't approach. It simply waits, and the night grows longer than the clock says. Beat: siege established.

chapters.title: Voices at the Windows
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The dead singers call from the garden in the voices of the living — Agnes, the washerwoman, Bram's sister — each inviting Noor to 'come sit.' Bram holds the line at the door, tallying aloud to keep himself anchored. Beat: loyalty tested against grief's counterfeits.

chapters.title: The Guest Speaks in Edith's Voice
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The Guest offers a bargain in Edith's voice: sit in the chair, and Edith's memory, name, and photographs will be restored; refuse, and the village feeds it for another century. Beat: the central temptation — loyalty versus truth made flesh.

chapters.title: The Long Middle of the Night
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Hours stretch. Noor reads Edith's notebooks aloud to stay herself, and the Guest answers with Edith's own marginalia, correcting her, intimate and patient. The chair in the photos is now in the room with her, hearth-lit. Beat: psychological attrition.

chapters.title: Bram's Door
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The Guest takes Bram's sister's shape at his threshold, and he nearly opens the door. He holds by reciting the true, ugly history of the pact aloud — truth as a ward. He is bleeding from the nose when dawn is still hours off. Beat: the cost of truth made literal.

chapters.title: What Noor Most Truly Holds
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor realizes what the Guest will take if she names it: not Edith — herself. Her name, her face, her place in every photograph and memory. The village would keep their pact's peace and forget she ever existed. Beat: the sacrifice clarified.

chapters.title: The Villagers Choose
chapters.summary: The vicar leads the village to Noor's gate at 3 a.m., asking — politely, terribly — that she sit in the chair, for the good of Marrowfen. Bram stands between them and the door. Beat: justice outside the law versus the mob's quiet arithmetic.

chapters.title: The Chair Is Pulled Out
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. In the photographs — and then in the room — the chair is drawn from the table, facing her, the Guest standing beside it with a courtesy like a butler's. The night has stopped moving toward sunrise. Beat: the trap fully sprung.

chapters.title: The Fourth Verse
chapters.summary: Noor opens the door herself, walks past the villagers, and stands before the Guest. She sings the fourth verse — the one that names the listener — aloud, complete, in Edith's collected notation. The village flinches as if struck. Beat: climax begins; the taboo broken.

chapters.title: Unwriting
chapters.summary: The Guest, named, begins to unmake the pact — and Noor with it. Photographs bleach, her chalk tallies vanish, Bram's face goes blank as he looks at her. Noor holds the last note, choosing to be forgotten rather than to let the debt pass on. Beat: sacrifice at the peak.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Dawn arrives for the first time in a night without end. The chair is gone from every photograph in Marrowfen; the famine-pact is a story with no terms. Bram stands in a cottage that belongs to no one he can name, holding a notebook he can't stop crying over. Beat: victory and erasure.

chapters.title: The Village After
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, thinning. The villagers begin singing the harvest song freely, all four verses, and the songs lose their power as the truth spreads. Noor feels herself fading from their telling — each retelling of the night omits her more. Beat: bittersweet liberation.

chapters.title: What Remains of a Name
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. In the last hour of her presence, Noor writes her own account into Edith's notebook — the only record that will hold — and leaves it for whoever counts doors next. Bram, the only one fighting to remember, presses her hand and says her name like a tally. Beat: farewell.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Weeks later, Marrowfen's photographs show only what was there. Bram keeps the cottage, keeps the notebook, and tells the story to anyone who will listen, always ending with the folklorist whose name he alone can still say. Beat: memory as the last act of justice.

chapters.title: A Song Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Noor's voice in the notebook's last pages, then Bram's coda. A traveler arrives in Marrowfen asking to record songs, and Bram, at the cottage door, sings the fourth verse twice — freely, in memory — and invites her in. The chair stays empty. Beat: the cycle broken, truth chosen over silence, and the reader left with the question of what we owe the dead and the forgotten.
